# Level 2 (progress 1/8) — model confirmed

## Geometry
Cell centers: x = 120+24c, y = 120+24r. Block 16px, pitch 24. Markers = 4 yellow 8px squares in diagonal gaps.

## Tracks (3, all cyclic)
- RING (26 cells): perimeter of rect rows r1..r10, cols c3..c7 (top row r1 c3..c7, right col c7 r2..r9, bottom row r10 c7..c3, left col c3 r9..r2).
  Index clockwise: 0=(r1,c3),1=(r1,c4),2=(r1,c5),3=(r1,c6),4=(r1,c7),5=(r2,c7)...12=(r9,c7),13=(r10,c7),14=(r10,c6)...17=(r10,c3),18=(r9,c3)...25=(r2,c3).
  RED arrow (168,144) => index-1 (top row moves left). GREEN arrow (312,144) => index+1.
- ROW A (r4): 10 cells c1..c10, cyclic. RED (120,216) shifts left, GREEN (384,216) shifts right. Shares (r4,c3)=ring23 and (r4,c7)=ring7.
- ROW B (r7): 10 cells c1..c10, cyclic. RED (120,288) left, GREEN (384,288) right. Shares (r7,c3)=ring20 and (r7,c7)=ring10.

## Targets
Markers at (r4,c7)=ring7 [M1] and (r7,c7)=ring10 [M2]. Two YELLOW blocks.
Parity: ring rotation preserves spacing; row transfer changes it by ±10 mod 26 => spacing parity invariant (even). Needed spacing 3 (odd) => both-at-once IMPOSSIBLE. So markers must lock/consume sequentially.

## State at turn 11
Yellow A at ring idx 2 (r1,c5); Yellow B at ring idx 18 (r9,c3).

## Plan (9 clicks)
1. GREEN ring (312,144) x2 -> A idx4, B idx20=(r7,c3)
2. GREEN rowB (384,288) x4 -> B to (r7,c7)=M2  [check for lock/consume]
3. GREEN ring (312,144) x3 -> A idx7 = M1

## Budget
Bar 8px per move this level (~64 moves). Used 2.

# Game model: "Yellow-to-marker" track puzzles (8 levels, ACTION6 only)

## Core rules (constant across all levels)
- Board = colored 16/32px blocks on a lattice; every block sits on one or more **cyclic tracks**.
- **Markers** = 4 small corner squares in the diagonal gaps around one cell. Marker colour = the block
  colour required there (yellow markers -> yellow block; orange markers -> orange block).
- **Goal of a level**: every marked cell holds a block of the marker's colour *simultaneously*
  (there is no locking/consuming; the win check is on the final state).
- **Arrow shapes are buttons** (click with ACTION6, centre of the shape):
  - red = "backward", green = "forward" (they are exact inverses).
  - For a straight line: red at the left/bottom end moves blocks left/down; green right/up.
  - For a ring: red = counter-clockwise (top row moves left), green = clockwise.
- Clicking blocks or empty space does nothing and costs no budget.
- **Budget bar** = full-height green bar at x0-8. It shrinks a fixed amount per *effective* move
  (L1: 40px = 13 moves; later levels 8px = 64 moves). Top bar = 8 level-progress segments.

## Track topologies seen (each level adds one)
1. One 20-cell ring; bring the unique yellow block to the marked ring cell.
2. Ring (26) + two 10-cell rows crossing it; cells shared by two tracks.
3. Two 16-cell octagon loops sharing 2 cells (transfer point).
4. Two long cyclic tracks only (H and V), each formed by *two* collinear arm groups joined by a
   wrap; all arrows of the same orientation drive the same track.
5. One 21-cell serpentine cycle + a 5-cell sub-track (top row) whose cells are shared with it.
6. Three 8-arm "snowflakes" (8 angles x 3 radii, empty centre): E-arrow = shift all arms outward
   (mod 3), S-arrow = rotate 45 deg CCW. A separate hub arrow swaps each snowflake's spoke-r3 cell
   with the adjacent marked cell (all 3 at once).
7. Gear-linked tracks: one arrow rotates *two* tracks at once (8-cell row + 4-cell ring);
   a third track (column) sharing one cell with the row is independent -> use it to "park" a block.
8. Three "elbow" tracks (diagonal then vertical column, last cell = its marker).
   One bottom arrow pair rotates ALL three tracks; three side pairs each rotate only the
   start segment (cells with x-index <= 7) of one track.

## Key solving techniques
- **Parking**: a block sitting on a cell of track A that is *not* on track B is immune to B's
  rotations. Move a block off the shared cell, rotate the other track, then bring it back.
  This defeats parity/offset obstructions (two blocks on one cycle keep a fixed separation).
- Compute each block's index on its cycle and solve the congruences
  (index + rotations + transfers) = target index, minimising total clicks.
- Prefer a global arrow that advances several targets at once; use per-track arrows only for
  the residual offsets. Ending with a single global move that lands everything is often shortest
  (e.g. L8: bring all yellows to index 0, then one backward global click puts each on its last cell).

## Measuring the board cheaply
- Sample cell centres with read_pixels: block interiors give the "fill" colour, exact centres often
  give a darker grid-line variant of the same hue (1:1 mapping, still distinguishable).
- Sample the *gap* centres (half-pitch offset) to find marker corners and their colour.
- Lattice: find pitch/offset with one 4px-resolution horizontal and vertical strip first.

**Game complete: WIN, 8/8 levels.**

Summary of what the game turned out to be and how it was solved:

- **Mechanic**: every level is a set of cyclic "tracks" of coloured blocks driven by red/green arrow buttons (red = backward/left/CCW, green = forward/right/CW). Yellow (or orange) corner markers mark target cells; the level completes when each marked cell simultaneously holds a block of the marker's colour.
- **Progression of topologies**: single ring → ring + crossing rows → two loops sharing cells → two long wrap-around tracks → serpentine cycle + sub-track → polar "snowflakes" + hub swap → gear-linked tracks + parking column → three elbow tracks with a global rotator.
- **Key insight reused repeatedly**: two blocks on one cycle keep a fixed separation, so offsets must be fixed by *parking* a block on a cell that belongs to only one track, rotating the other track, then re-inserting it.
- **Efficiency**: level solutions were computed as congruences before acting (e.g. the final level was finished in 9 clicks by aligning all three yellows at index 0 and applying one global backward rotation), keeping well inside each level's move budget.
